title: BTS’ Grammy Decision: Was the Band Getting Ahead of Another Awards Show Sidelining? (Critic’s Take)
summary: The group's decision isn't a snub; it's recognition of a pattern the group has been navigating for years.
contentText:
On Wednesday (July 29), the seven members of BTS posted to their individual Instagram accounts a short, identical and pointedly undramatic statement : They will not submit their music for consideration at the upcoming 69th Grammy Awards. They shared their hope that “music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language.” No category was named and there was no mention of past Grammy experiences. BTS’ management company HYBE later clarified that this is “not a company-wide boycott” and neither the group nor the label asked anyone else to follow.

Related

Grammys Chief Responds to BTS’ Decision To Not Enter Its Songs for Consideration at 2027 Grammys

HUNTR/X’s ‘Golden’ Marks First-Ever K-Pop Grammy Win

The restraint is telling as BTS have long expressed their admiration and respect for the Grammys as an institution. This is not an artist reacting to a snub, but rather BTS recognizing the importance of making a statement before history repeats itself.

In July 2019, the MTV Video Music Awards announced a new category, best K-pop, arriving after a period during which BTS had rewritten YouTube’s record books without a single nomination to show for it. At that point, BTS had already broken the record for the most-watched music video within 24 hours on the platform, with “IDOL” garnering 45.9 million views in August 2018, and it went on to become the fastest music video that year to surpass 100 million views on YouTube. Those stats put BTS squarely alongside artists like Eminem , Taylor Swift and Ariana Grande , all of whom already had multiple wins at the VMAs in long-standing categories like video of the year for both Em and Swift, while Grande had two wins for best pop video.

When BTS’ recognition finally came, it arrived in a new category — one many saw as being built specifically to hold them. Of course, BTS won the award for best K-pop for their “Boy With Luv” music video featuring Halsey (which also rewrote the 24-hour YouTube record with 74.6 million views in a day), as well as the fan-voted best group category. What they did not receive was a nod in any of the ceremony’s long-running marquee races. How they could corral the most excitement and attention for any music video that year, but not even be listed as a potential contender for video or pop video of the year at the world’s biggest music video ceremony?

Yes, we're still running the numbers, but we can confirm that #BoyWithLuv (ft. @Halsey ) is now *officially* the most-viewed 24 hour debut in @YouTube history!! Congratulations @bts_bighit 🎉 Enjoy @nbcsnl tonight! pic.twitter.com/xC8vHs27Nu

— YouTube Music (@youtubemusic) April 14, 2019

Perhaps aware of some of the fan and media discourse over best K-pop, MTV did nominate BTS in a main VMA category in 2020 when “ON” competed in best pop — the first for the group and the first for any Asian artist in the show’s history — alongside such artists as Jonas Brothers, Lady Gaga and Justin Bieber. BTS took home the best pop and best K-pop trophies, plus the technical award of best choreography and the fan-voted best group. The specialized category had to arrive first before the general one opened.

To BTS’ many fans, it sometimes seems like the Western industry has a habit of building an annex when confronted with music it cannot ignore and has not made room for, rather than widening the room itself.

Other award shows made their own version of that same call. Since 2020, similar fan-focused award shows including the American Music Awards, MTV Europe Music Awards and iHeartRadio Music Awards have added K-pop-specific categories, as have the data-driven Billboard Music Awards. In many cases, songs recorded entirely in English — or by acts that are not even Korean — are still recognized only in the K-pop bracket. The most recent best K-pop VMA went to “Born Again” by Thailand-born LISA of BLACKPINK with Doja Cat and RAYE, an all-English single that was LISA’s lone nomination that night and one plainly worthy of consideration in best pop or best collaboration. In every case, the intention was almost certainly to be generous and to respond to the growing impact of the Korean music industry. Still, many wondered whether the ultimate effect would silo these artists from the larger pop music conversation.

For their part, BTS did not opt out of this system but publicly committed to it for years. Between 2021 and 2023, the septet collected five Grammy nominations: three straight in best pop duo/group performance for “Dynamite,” “Butter” and “My Universe,” the latter a collab with longtime Grammy favorites Coldplay, plus best music video for “Yet to Come” and an album of the year credit as featured artists on Coldplay’s Music of the Spheres . They presented awards, performed on the telecast three years running (once in tandem with other acts), and were invited to serve as voting members of the Recording Academy in 2019. They called the Grammy their “last summit “ left to climb. They also lost, gracefully, five times.

This past February, K-pop had its biggest night ever at the Grammys. Billboard Hot 100 No. 1 hit “Golden” from KPop Demon Hunters became the first song from the K-pop scene to win a Grammy when it won best song written for visual media. BLACKPINK’s ROSÉ opened the show after becoming the first K-pop soloist nominated in the general field, thanks to “APT.” with Bruno Mars, a record and song of the year nominee. HYBE’s global girl group KATSEYE was up for best new artist and best pop duo/group performance. The ceremony demonstrated in real time that the existing categories were perfectly capable of holding this music scene and the different ways it was extending internationally.

Four months after its 2026 telecast, the Recording Academy announced the newly added best Asian pop music performance category, which privately confused those close to these industries. Its official description says eligible recordings “typically feature melody-driven composition, mainstream pop songwriting, and commercially oriented production,” often marked by “genre-blending arrangements, layered production, and dynamic structural shifts.” Remove the “Asian” geography and that could describe nearly every record nominated in the pop performance categories.

The one criterion that actually narrows the field is language. Recordings “must feature meaningful use of one or more Asian languages,” and anything performed entirely in English is explicitly ruled out — though the Academy notes those songs remain eligible elsewhere, and that musical style, not a performer’s nationality, governs eligibility. While the description leaves unresolved whether the Indian subcontinent or the Middle East is included, it also specifically spotlights K-pop, J-pop and C-pop as three major East Asian industries whose pop music outputs have little in common sonically except the region they originate from.

Specifically, that language test is even trickier than it first appears. An official description stipulates that only one version of a recording can compete in a performance category in a given year, and that a recording “entered in another performance category is not also eligible in best Asian pop music performance for a different version featuring an Asian language performance.”

Run ARIRANG through those rules and the choices become mostly clearer. “SWIM,” the Hot 100-topping lead single performed entirely in English, is ineligible for the new category and…
